[THOUGHT] The focal, progressive right upper‑extremity weakness predominantly affecting the hand/fingers with neuropathic burning/aching pain and sensory loss is most consistent with lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) involvement. Examination lacks UMN signs, fasciculations, or marked atrophy, arguing against ALS; the deficit is unilateral and focal, which is atypical for diabetic or alcoholic peripheral neuropathy (which are symmetric, distal, sensory‑predominant). Cervical radiculopathy is possible but Spurling’s and neck provocative testing were negative and the pattern (severe intrinsic hand weakness with sensory loss and neuropathic pain) is classic for brachial plexus invasion. The chest X‑ray and CT show a solid apical (right) lung mass — the hallmark of a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor that commonly invades the lower brachial plexus producing pain, sensory loss and weakness of hand muscles. Pending EMG/NCS would localize the lesion to the plexus, but the combination of focal hand weakness + neuropathic pain + right apical lung mass makes a Pancoast tumor with brachial plexopathy the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor of the right lung causing invasion of the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) — i.e., Pancoast tumor–associated brachial plexopathy.

[THOUGHT] The clinical picture is a progressive, focal, painful right hand/arm paresis with sensory loss localizing to the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1/distribution of intrinsic hand muscles). This pattern—severe neuropathic arm pain followed by focal intrinsic hand weakness—is classic for involvement of the lower brachial plexus by an apical (superior sulcus, “Pancoast”) process. The chest imaging documents a right apical solid mass consistent with an apical lung tumor, which provides a direct anatomic explanation for brachial plexus involvement. Absence of Horner’s features does not exclude a Pancoast lesion (Horner’s occurs only if sympathetic chain is affected). Normal NCS/EMG and a normal brachial-plexus MRI can occur early in the course or with focal/patchy tumor invasion not captured on imaging, and PET and biopsy can be falsely negative because of sampling error or low FDG-avidity histology. Other alternatives (ALS, diabetic or alcoholic polyneuropathy, peripheral entrapment, cervical radiculopathy, stroke) do not fit the focal, painful, lower-plexus pattern with a concordant apical lung mass. Therefore, despite some normal ancillary tests, the single most likely diagnosis is an apical (Pancoast) lung tumor causing invasion of the lower brachial plexus (Pancoast tumor–associated brachial plexopathy).

[DIAGNOSIS] Right Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor of the lung causing invasion of the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) — Pancoast tumor–associated brachial plexopathy.

- Tissue diagnosis (biopsy) of the apical mass to confirm malignancy and histology.
- Focused exam for Horner syndrome (ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis) which commonly accompanies Pancoast tumors.
